notes.meaning: Samuel passed away after many faithful years of guiding God's people, and the whole nation gathered to mourn and bury him at his home in Ramah. With his great counselor gone, David felt his danger from Saul more deeply and moved south into the wilderness of Paran. Even when an important spiritual leader dies, God continues to protect and guide his people.

A wealthy man lived in Maon and kept his large flocks of sheep and goats in nearby Carmel. His name was Nabal, which means "fool," and he was known for being stubborn, rude, and dishonest. In contrast, his wife Abigail was both wise and beautiful, living in a difficult marriage with a man who failed to live up to the noble heritage of his ancestor Caleb.

While living in the wilderness, David learned that Nabal was shearing his sheep. Sheep-shearing season was like harvest time for flock owners. It was traditionally celebrated with bountiful food, high spirits, and generous hospitality to guests.

David sent ten of his young men to Carmel to greet Nabal with great courtesy and respect. They were instructed to wish Nabal long life and peace, praying for God's blessing on him, his family, and everything he owned. David approached him not with threats, but with sincere kindness.

David reminded Nabal that his men had lived peacefully alongside Nabal's shepherds without taking a single animal or doing any harm. Since it was a festive feast day, David politely asked if Nabal would share whatever food was on hand with his men. He did not demand supplies as a tax, but humbly asked as a son seeking fatherly goodwill.

David's messengers arrived and delivered their leader's respectful request word for word. After speaking, they sat down and waited quietly for Nabal's answer. They expected a friendly response in keeping with the hospitality of the harvest season.

Nabal answered with cruel insults, pretending he did not know who David was and sneering that many runaway slaves were fleeing their masters. He stingily claimed all the bread, water, and meat as solely his own property. Instead of showing gratitude, he used insults as an excuse to avoid helping people in need.

David's young men turned around and walked back to their camp to report Nabal's rude words. They showed great self-control by refusing to trade insults or take food by force. Instead, they let David decide how to handle the situation.

David flew into a sudden rage upon hearing the insult and commanded four hundred of his men to strap on their swords. He left two hundred men behind to guard their camp supplies and set off to attack Nabal. Although David had shown great patience with King Saul, he lost his temper here and failed to seek God's counsel before marching.

One of the household servants went straight to Abigail to tell her what had happened. He explained that David had sent messengers offering peaceful greetings, but Nabal had screamed and hurled insults at them. The servant knew Abigail had the good sense that her husband lacked.

The servant testified that David's men had been wonderful neighbors while the flocks grazed out in the open country. Rather than stealing or causing harm, David's fighters had stood like a protective wall around the shepherds day and night against bandits and wild animals. Their discipline and care had kept Nabal's entire livelihood safe.

The servant urged Abigail to think quickly about what to do, because terrible disaster was about to fall on their master and the entire household. He knew it was useless to talk to Nabal directly, because Nabal was so bad-tempered that no one could reason with him. The servant trusted Abigail's wisdom to find a way of escape.

Abigail moved quickly and gathered a generous feast of bread, wine skins, butchered sheep, roasted grain, raisins, and pressed fig cakes onto pack donkeys. She sent her servants ahead with the food and promised to follow right behind them, but she told Nabal nothing. She took this bold step without his permission to save her family from total destruction.

As Abigail rode her donkey down through a hidden mountain ravine, David and his four hundred men came marching down the opposite slope right toward her. God arranged the timing so that they met face-to-face before any violence could take place. Her sudden arrival placed her directly between David and his planned revenge.

As David marched, he had been bitterly complaining that his faithful protection of Nabal's goods in the desert had been entirely wasted. In blind fury over being repaid evil for good, David swore a reckless curse before God to slaughter every male in Nabal's household before sunrise. This murderous vow shows how quickly even a godly leader can give in to ungodly anger when he relies on his own feelings.
